title: The Art of Foresight
author: Ian Hallett
summary: This article, part of The Art of Leadership series, contrasts Nvidia's twenty-year bet on parallel computing with Intel's failure to look beyond its dominant CPU business, using both as case studies in the presence or absence of organizational foresight. Foresight is not prediction — it is pattern recognition applied to structural changes already in motion but not yet visible in results. Three reasons make foresight rare: the present is noisy while the future is quiet, foresight requires acting before evidence is conclusive, and success actively blinds leaders to the structural shifts that will displace them. The author presents a practical discipline for building foresight: separating structural changes from noise, looking where nobody else is looking, tracking academic research, asking the ten-year question deliberately, and investing before it is comfortable. Foresight is disciplined and patient, not fashionable — it means committing to a small number of deep structural changes and building around them for years.
points: Foresight is not prediction but pattern recognition applied to structural changes already in motion — leaders don't need a crystal ball, they need discipline to identify deep currents and courage to build toward them.

Three forces make foresight rare: the noisy present crowds out the quiet future; acting before evidence is conclusive is uncomfortable; and success in the current business actively blinds leaders to what will replace it.

A structural change has three properties: it has been building for years, it crosses multiple industries, and it is driven by deep forces (technological, demographic, economic, or regulatory) that will not reverse.
The most valuable foresight rarely comes from analyzing the same variables as competitors more skillfully; it comes from noticing a change that sits outside the frame everyone else is using.

Foresight without commitment is just observation; the whole point is to allocate real capital and talent to a structural change while it still feels early — that discomfort is the price of a leading position.
quotes: Foresight is not prediction. Prediction is trying to guess what will happen: who wins the election, where interest rates land, which product takes off. Prediction is mostly a mug’s game, and leaders who stake their strategy on specific predictions usually get burned.
Foresight is different. Foresight is pattern recognition applied to structural changes that are already in motion but have not yet impacted in your results.

The structural changes that will reshape your industry over the next decade are almost always visible today, if you know how to look. They are just not yet urgent, which is precisely why most firms ignore them.
The most valuable foresight rarely comes from analysing the same variables as your competitors more skilfully. It comes from noticing a change that sits outside the frame everyone else is using.
Foresight is disciplined, not fashionable. It means committing to a small number of deep structural changes and building around them for years, not lurching toward whatever is trending this month.

If your firm is not exercising foresight, someone else will exercise it on your behalf. A regulator. An investor. An acquirer. A government. And you will spend the next decade executing someone else’s judgement about your future.

You do not need a crystal ball. You need the discipline to identify the deep currents that are already flowing in your own industry, and the courage to build for where they lead, even when the destination is not yet visible in your results.
